seq: That was Mike Williams, the chief electronics technician on the Deepwater Horizon, testifying three months later. The call he described was on the night of April twentieth, twenty ten.
The rig was drilling in the Gulf of Mexico, about fifty miles off Louisiana. A hundred and twenty-six people were on board.
Earlier that evening, the crew had tested whether the well was sealed.
The readings contradicted each other. One line showed no flow. The drill pipe, open to the same well, showed fourteen hundred psi.
Around eight o'clock, the test was declared a success.
The presidential commission later concluded that the pressure could only have come from a leak into the well, and called the decision a key error.
Williams told investigators why the gas announcement that night did not alarm him.
By his account, the call was around nine thirty. At about nine forty, mud and gas burst onto the rig floor. Minutes later, the rig exploded.
Investigators would spend years asking how the well had been judged safe, and why the blowout preventer on the seafloor did not stop it.
